scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In the mountain village of Yatsuo, young unmarried dancers hide their faces beneath low-brimmed straw hats to appease the wrath of the wind gods.
This is Kaze no bon. Genroku era (1688-1704) to present.
on_screen: Title card: Kaze no bon · Japan · Genroku era (1688-1704) to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Kaze-no-Bon has a history of about 300 years, existing without interruption since the Genroku era (1688-1704).
The original festival was held in order to honor Shinto divinities and appease typhoons so that they would spare the upcoming rice harvest in early September.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Held annually from September 1 to 3, the festival serves to appease wind and typhoon gods.
The dancers hide their faces to protect themselves from the wrath of the gods they hope to appease.

Traditionally, performers were strictly unmarried, rooted in ideas of virginal self-sacrifice to avoid angering the deities, though modern interpretations also view it as a chance for young people to meet.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Young men and women progress slowly in long parallel files through the streets, dancing simultaneously to a melody.
Each troupe represents one of the eleven districts of Yatsuo.
The traditional style is Kyu odori, while Shin odori was introduced in 1920, featuring distinct steps for men and women where the men's movements evoke agricultural field work.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: At the rear of the procession, a well-aged female voice sings Ecchu Owara Bushi, a traditional village song.
This voice is accompanied by rare instruments including the kokyū (a traditional stringed vièle), the traditional shamisen (a three-stringed lute), and drums.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The festival takes place at night in the steep, cobbled center of Yatsuo village, which spans the Ida river between two mountains.
The streets are decorated with paper lanterns.
Dancers wear matching cotton yukata and flat straw hats called amigasa, which are tilted to cover their faces.
